approach: The authors conducted a systematic review following PRISMA guidelines. They searched PubMed and Cochrane databases for peer-reviewed articles published between December 2015 and December 2024. Inclusion criteria covered randomized/non-randomized clinical trials in humans and animal models investigating the association between microbiome and TNBC treatment response. Data extraction focused on study design, population, interventions, and key findings. Risk of bias was assessed using ROBINS-I, ROB 2, and SYRCLE tools depending on study type. The results were narratively synthesized by grouping studies into human clinical/translational cohorts and murine/preclinical mechanistic models.

contribution_and_limits.contribution: Provides a comprehensive narrative synthesis of both clinical and preclinical evidence linking microbiome features (diversity, specific taxa, metabolites) to TNBC treatment outcomes (pCR, PFS, OS).
contribution_and_limits.limits: Narrative synthesis only; no meta-analysis performed. Included studies vary widely in design, sample size, and sequencing methods. Many clinical studies have small sample sizes or are retrospective. Causal mechanisms are largely inferred from preclinical data or correlative clinical observations.

key_findings.finding: Higher baseline gut microbiome alpha-diversity (Shannon index) is significantly associated with achieving pCR (Vernaci et al., 2023). Specific taxa like Bacteroides eggerthii were enriched in responders.

High baseline Faith's phylogenetic diversity (PD) predicts prolonged progression-free survival (PFS), particularly in the atezolizumab arm (ALICE trial). Bifidobacterium enrichment was associated with lack of clinical benefit in this specific context.

Cumulative antimicrobial exposure is associated with decreased overall survival (OS) and breast cancer-specific survival (BCS), independent of stage and ANC. This effect persists for up to 3 years post-diagnosis.

Higher intratumoral bacterial burden correlates with pCR to neoadjuvant chemoimmunotherapy. High load is associated with increased FOLR2+ macrophages and decreased SPP1+ (immunosuppressive) macrophages.

Gut microbiota depletion (antibiotics/germ-free) attenuates doxorubicin efficacy and CD8+ T cell infiltration; fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) restores response. Engineered E. coli producing methioninase reduces tumor growth via methionine depletion. Microbial metabolite TMAO promotes anti-PD-1 efficacy via GSDME-mediated pyroptosis.

problem_or_question: Does the microbiome influence pathological response and clinical outcomes in TNBC patients undergoing standard systemic therapies (chemotherapy and immunotherapy)?
research_scope: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC); gut and tumor-associated microbiome; neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NACT) and immune checkpoint blockade (ICB).
work_summary: This systematic review synthesizes evidence from 14 studies (clinical trials, observational cohorts, and preclinical models) to evaluate the role of the microbiome in TNBC therapeutic response. It specifically investigates whether baseline microbiome composition and diversity predict pathological complete response (pCR) or survival outcomes under NACT and ICB regimens. The review highlights that higher microbial diversity and specific commensal taxa are associated with enhanced antitumor immunity and better treatment efficacy, while antibiotic-induced dysbiosis correlates with poorer outcomes. It also discusses potential mechanisms involving immune cell infiltration, macrophage polarization, and microbial metabolites.
